title: Make Or Break
author: Carli Brosseau
summary: Carli Brosseau reports a data investigation, produced with Big Local News at Stanford and The Hechinger Report, showing that North Carolina holds ninth graders back at nearly the highest rate in the country, more than double the national figure and consistently above it since well before the pandemic. Her argument is that the state has concentrated its retention in the grade where the practice does the most damage, since the research base that offers partial support for early elementary retention does not extend to older students, and being held back is closely associated with dropping out. The piece then shows why the rate is so uneven: the triggers for retention vary by grade, district and sometimes individual school, with a third grade literacy law full of superintendent-controlled exceptions, principal discretion elsewhere, and district credit, attendance and even community service requirements in high school. Brosseau documents that Black, Hispanic and Native American students are retained at roughly twice the rate of white students and that Black boys fare worst, tracing the pattern to discipline disparities, teacher assignment, segregation and the resource gaps of poor rural districts. Against that she profiles A&T Four Middle College in Greensboro, whose summer bridge program, small classes, two-year teacher pairings and accessible principal have lifted proficiency rates for Black and Hispanic boys. The uncomfortable conclusion is that the model works and is being defunded, with tutor positions lost, coaching days cut, and counselors carrying caseloads far above recommended ratios.
points: More than one in ten North Carolina ninth graders failed to meet promotion requirements in 2021-22, more than double the national rate, and the state has run above the national figure every year federal data is available since 2011-12.

Retention triggers are radically inconsistent: the 2012 literacy law governs third grade with superintendent-approved exceptions, principals decide other grades, and districts set their own credit, attendance and even community service rules for high school.

Black, Hispanic and Native American students are about twice as likely to be retained as white students, boys are 38 percent more likely than girls, and Black boys are held back at the highest rates of all.

Brosseau links the gaps to exclusionary discipline and teacher distribution, citing a federal finding that Winston-Salem Forsyth suspended Black students at three to four times the rate of white students for comparable behavior.

A&T Four Middle College shows what prevention costs: a small all-boys magnet with a summer bridge program, two-year teacher pairings and a counselor who meets students in middle school, all funded by grants the principal has to negotiate for each year.
quotes: North Carolina ninth graders fail to fulfill the requirements to advance to 10th grade at one of the highest rates in the country, according to an analysis of data from the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights by Big Local News at Stanford University in partnership with The Hechinger Report and The Assembly.

In the 2021-22 school year—the most recent for which federal data is available—more than 1 in 10 ninth graders here had to repeat or make up a portion of the year’s schoolwork to advance under their district’s rules. That’s more than double the national rate.

But because holding students back is “highly associated with dropouts,” the ninth-grade figures warrant some concern, said Sarah Crittenden Fuller, a research associate professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who included retention rates in an examination of the pandemic’s effect on North Carolina students.
Schools in the South tend to hold back students at higher rates than in other regions; they also tend to spend less per pupil than the national average.
Retention “can cause a student a lot of anxiety, a lot of stress, and it can also cause some students to not return to school because their self-esteem takes a hit,” she said.
In North Carolina, the triggers for retaining a student vary by grade, district, and sometimes even school.

Black, Hispanic, and Native American students in North Carolina were about twice as likely to be held back as the state’s white students, and boys were 38% more likely than girls, Big Local News found. Black boys were retained at the highest rates of all.

If students are going to have some challenges in a class or a year of transition,” she said, “it is that ninth-grade year.” On the flip side, research suggests that if students end freshman year on track, they are three times as likely to graduate.
